On deciding transcendence of power series

Alin Bostan Alin BostanInria, Sorbonne Université, LIP6, F-75252 Paris, France Email address: alin.bostan@inria.fr , Bruno Salvy Bruno SalvyInria, CNRS, ENS de Lyon, Université Claude Bernard Lyon 1, LIP, UMR 5668, 69342 Lyon Cedex 07, France Email address: bruno.salvy@inria.fr and Michael F. Singer Michael F. SingerDepartment of Mathematics, North Carolina State University, Box 8205, Raleigh, NC 27695, USA Email address: singer@ncsu.edu
Date: September 17, 2026
Abstract.

It is well known that algebraic power series are differentially finite (D-finite): they satisfy linear differential equations with polynomial coefficients. The converse problem—determining whether a given D-finite power series is algebraic or transcendental—is notoriously difficult. We prove that this problem is decidable: we give two theoretical algorithms and a transcendence test that results in an efficient Maple implementation.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
11J81, 16S32, 34M15

1. Introduction

1.1. Stanley’s problem and our contribution

A power series f∈ℚ⁡[[z]]f\in{\mathbb{Q}}[[z]] is called algebraic if it is a root of some polynomial equation P⁡(z,f⁡(z))=0P(z,f(z))=0, where P∈ℚ⁡[x,y]∖{0}P\in\mathbb{Q}[x,y]\setminus\{0\}; otherwise, ff is called transcendental. A classical result, known to Abel (1827) and possibly much older, states that any algebraic power series f∈ℚ⁡[[z]]f\in{\mathbb{Q}}[[z]] is D-finite (or, differentially finite)—that is, it satisfies a linear differential equation with coefficients in ℚ⁡[z]{\mathbb{Q}}[z]. Moreover, the minimal-order nontrivial homogeneous linear differential equation satisfied by ff has order at most degy⁡(P)\deg_{y}(P) and coefficients in ℚ⁡[z]{\mathbb{Q}}[z] of degree at most 4​degx⁡(P)​degy​(P)24\deg_{x}(P)\deg_{y}(P)^{2} [13].

Conversely, not every D-finite power series is algebraic; for instance, exp⁡(z)\exp(z) and log⁡(1−z)\log(1-z) are both D-finite and transcendental. Several methods are available to prove the transcendence of exp⁡(z)\exp(z) and log⁡(1−z)\log(1-z) (see e.g., [12]), but in general it is notoriously difficult to decide if a given D-finite function is algebraic or transcendental. This is the topic of our article.

In his seminal article on D-finite functions [103, §4, (g), page 186], Richard Stanley asked the following question:

“Given the differential equation

(1) L⁡(f⁡(z))=ar​(z)​f(r)​(z)+⋯+a0​(z)​f​(z)=0{L}(f(z))=a_{r}(z)f^{(r)}(z)+\dots+a_{0}(z)f(z)=0

with polynomial coefficients ai∈ℚ⁡[z]a_{i}\in{\mathbb{Q}}[z], together with suitable (finitely many) initial conditions, satisfied by a D-finite power series ff, give an algorithm suitable for computer implementation for deciding whether ff is algebraic.”

For instance, f⁡(z)≔∑n≥1zn/nf(z)\coloneq\sum_{n\geq 1}z^{n}/n is a D-finite power series represented by the second-order differential equation (z−1)​f′′​(z)+f′​(z)=0(z-1)f^{\prime\prime}(z)+f^{\prime}(z)=0 and initial conditions f⁡(0)=0,f′​(0)=1f(0)=0,f^{\prime}(0)=1, and such an algorithm would have to recognize the transcendence of ff starting from this data alone.

Deciding transcendence of formal power series has many motivations and applications. For instance, in number theory a first step towards proving the transcendence of a complex number consists in proving the transcendence of some suitable power series attached to it. Other examples come from combinatorics, where the nature of generating functions may reveal strong underlying structures [15], and from computer science, where a natural question is whether algebraic power series are easier to manipulate than transcendental ones [9].

Although Stanley insisted on the practical aspect of the targeted algorithm for deciding algebraicity of D-finite functions, not even a theoretical one has appeared so far. In this work, we make progress on Stanley’s question: we give two algorithms that prove the decidability of the algebraic or transcendental nature of D-finite power series in ℚ⁡[[z]]{\mathbb{Q}}[[z]] and we give an (incomplete) transcendence test whose implementation is efficient in practice.

The first theoretical algorithm (Algorithm 1) relies on minimization of linear differential equations [18]; the second one (Algorithm 5) uses factorization. Both rely on Singer’s algorithm [96]. The practical transcendence test (Algorithm 2) combines the same minimization as the first algorithm with a local analysis; it is incomplete in the sense that it is guaranteed to be correct only when it returns “transcendental”. If the input differential equation possesses additional properties (e.g., if it annihilates the diagonal of a multivariate rational function [25]), then a variant of it (Algorithm 3) is also guaranteed to be correct when it returns “algebraic”, modulo a conjecture in the theory of arithmetic differential equations (Conjecture 10). Designing complete and efficient algebraicity or transcendence tests is still open.

1.2. Difficulties and analogies

There are several a priori reasons why Stanley’s problem is difficult. First, the minimal polynomial of an algebraic power series f⁡(z)f(z) may have arbitrarily large size (degrees) with respect to the size (order/degree) of its defining differential equation. For instance, f⁡(z)=1−zNf(z)=\sqrt[N]{1-z} has algebraicity degree NN and satisfies the first-order differential equation N⁡(z−1)​f′​(z)−f⁡(z)=0N(z-1)f^{\prime}(z)-f(z)=0. Second, no characterization is available for coefficient sequences of algebraic power series; this is in contrast with the smaller class of rational functions (whose coefficient sequences are C-recursive, i.e., satisfy linear recursions with constant coefficients) and with the larger class of D-finite functions (whose coefficient sequences are P-recursive, i.e., satisfy linear recursions with polynomial coefficients)11 1 Note that for the class of diagonals of rational functions, which is intermediate between algebraic and D-finite power series, coefficient sequences correspond (conjecturally) to the class of P-recursive sequences with (almost) integer coefficients and geometric growth (this is predicted by the “Christol conjecture”, see Part (1) of Conjecture 10)..

There are several analogies between the problems of transcendence in ℚ⁡[[z]]\mathbb{Q}[[z]] and of irreducibility in ℚ⁡[z]\mathbb{Q}[z]. One is that “generic” power series in ℚ⁡[[z]]\mathbb{Q}[[z]] are transcendental, much like “generic” polynomials in ℚ⁡[z]\mathbb{Q}[z] are irreducible. Another one is that, while many sufficient criteria exist (e.g., Eisenstein’s criteria for polynomial irreducibility [34], see also [94, 93, 30], and for power series transcendence, see Section 1.4.1), none of them is also necessary. This is closely related to the fact that there are no known characterizations at the level of the coefficient sequence for recognizing either irreducibility in ℚ⁡[z]{\mathbb{Q}}[z], or transcendence in ℚ⁡[[z]]{\mathbb{Q}}[[z]]. However, since polynomial irreducibility is known to be decidable [68, 71], it is legitimate to hope, by analogy, that the same holds for transcendence of power series.

1.3. Related problems

Although Stanley’s question is quite recent, it is related to many classical questions and results, dating back to the beginning of the 19th century.

Given a linear differential operator L=∑i=0rai(z)∂ziL=\sum_{i=0}^{r}a_{i}(z)\partial_{z}^{i} (where ∂z\partial_{z} stands for dd​z\frac{d}{dz}) with coefficients in ℚ⁡[z]\mathbb{Q}[z], modeling the linear differential equation (1), one may ask several questions concerning the algebraic nature over ℚ⁡(z)\mathbb{Q}(z) of its solutions:

  1. (F)

    Decide if all solutions of LL are algebraic (Fuchs’ problem).

  2. (L)

    Decide if LL admits at least one nontrivial algebraic solution (Liouville’s problem).

  3. (S)

    Decide if a given nonzero solution ff of LL is algebraic (Stanley’s problem).

Remark 1.

In problems (F) and (L) an “algebraic solution” of LL is an element ff of the field of formal Puiseux series 𝒫=⋃n∈ℕ⋆ℚ¯​((z1n))\mathcal{P}=\bigcup_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{\star}}{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}((z^{\frac{1}{n}})), such that ff is algebraic over ℚ⁡(z)\mathbb{Q}(z) and L⁡(f)=0L(f)=0. (Here ℚ¯{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}} is the algebraic closure of ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}.)

“All solutions of LL are algebraic” means that LL admits a full basis, i.e., a linearly independent family of cardinality r=ord⁡(L)r={\operatorname{ord}}(L), of solutions in 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

Note also that if LL is irreducible22 2 This means that LL cannot be written L=L1​L2L=L_{1}L_{2} in the (non-commutative) ring ℚ(z)⟨∂z⟩\mathbb{Q}(z)\langle\partial_{z}\rangle of linear differential operators, with 1≤ord⁡(L2)<r=ord⁡(L)1\leq{\operatorname{ord}}(L_{2})<r={\operatorname{ord}}(L). Irreducibility of linear differential operators was first studied by Frobenius (1873), and then uniqueness properties for factorization into irreducible operators were further studied by Landau (1902) and Loewy (1903). For historical accounts on the rich structural analogy between polynomials and linear differential equations, we refer to [32], [99, §2.4] and [14, p. 100], and the references therein. , then the three problems (F), (L) and (S) are equivalent. This is because an irreducible operator either admits a full basis of algebraic solutions, or no nontrivial algebraic solution, see [96, Prop. 2.5].

Above, the word “decide” may have several meanings. One may for instance ask for a criterion, that is for a mathematical characterization based on the inspection of the coefficients of LL, or of some invariants of LL (such as its singularities, exponents at singularities, etc.33 3 Finite singularities (or singular points) of Eq. 1 are points where one of the rational functions ai​(z)/ar​(z)a_{i}(z)/a_{r}(z) has a pole. Infinity is also a singular point when 0 is a singularity of the equation obtained by making the change of variables z↦1/zz\mapsto 1/z. For more information, see [59, §15.1].). The classical meaning in computer science—the one that we adopt in this article—is that one asks for an algorithmic decision procedure, which, on every specific instance of LL, is able to answer the given problem using a finite number of operations (++, ×\times, ÷\div, ==) in ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}.

In addition to such a decision procedure, one may also want to exhibit an annihilating polynomial (usually, the minimal polynomial) of the algebraic solution(s). Computing such a polynomial yields the most obvious “algebraicity witness”, on which the decision procedure itself may rely (see Section 4.2). However, these witnesses may have prohibitively large sizes; deciding algebraicity of solutions does not necessarily need them.

In this article, we add one more problem to the previous list:

  1. (P)

    Compute the (monic) right factor44 4 This is a linear differential operator with coefficients in ℚ⁡(z)\mathbb{Q}(z), see Proposition 3. LalgL^{\mathrm{alg}} of LL whose solution space is spanned by the algebraic solutions of LL.

Again, if LL is irreducible, then (P) is equivalent to the problems (F), (L) and (S).

Note that a solution to (P) implies solutions to each of the problems (F), (L) and (S). Indeed, solving (F), (L), and (S) amounts, respectively, to checking ord⁡(L)=ord⁡(Lalg){\operatorname{ord}}(L)={\operatorname{ord}}(L^{\mathrm{alg}}), resp. Lalg≠1L^{\mathrm{alg}}\neq 1, or Lalg​(f)=0L^{\mathrm{alg}}(f)=0 (the last equality can be checked as explained in [18, Lemma 2.1]).

1.4. Sufficient transcendence criteria

There exist several criteria that can be used to prove that a given power series f∈ℚ⁡[[z]]f\in{\mathbb{Q}}[[z]] is transcendental. They are simply built on properties of algebraic power series. We recall below two important ones, Eisenstein’s arithmetic criterion and Flajolet’s analytic criterion. Although very useful in practice, none of these sufficient criteria is also necessary, and there are concrete examples that escape them (see Example 6). This observation brings additional motivation to Stanley’s problem (S).

1.4.1. Eisenstein’s criterion

Definition 2.

A power series f=∑n≥0an​znf=\sum_{n\geq 0}a_{n}z^{n} in ℚ⁡[[z]]{\mathbb{Q}}[[z]] is called globally bounded if it has a non-zero and finite radius of convergence, and if there exists C∈ℕ∗C\in\mathbb{N}^{*} such that an​Cn∈ℤa_{n}C^{n}\in\mathbb{Z} for all n≥1n\geq 1.

A famous criterion, stated (and sketchily proved) in 1852 by Gotthold Eisenstein [35] and fully proved one year later by Eduard Heine [52], asserts that if a power series f∈ℚ⁡[[z]]f\in{\mathbb{Q}}[[z]] is algebraic, then only a finite number of prime numbers can divide the denominators of the coefficient sequence (an)n≥0(a_{n})_{n\geq 0}. This is also a consequence of a theorem55 5 Heine’s 1854 result is what is commonly called “Eisenstein’s criterion” in the literature. Hence, strictly speaking there are two distinct criteria, one due to Eisenstein and the other one due to Heine. It might well be that they coincide for D-finite functions; this is related to Siegel’s conjecture that the classes of “broad GG-functions” and “strict GG-functions” coincide, see e.g., [3, Conj. 2.3.1]. by Heine [53] stating that any algebraic power series f∈ℚ⁡[[z]]f\in{\mathbb{Q}}[[z]] is globally bounded. This arithmetic criterion immediately implies that the power series log(1−z)=−∑n≥1zn/n\log(1-z)=-\sum_{n\geq 1}z^{n}/n (more generally, the polylogarithm Lis​(z)=∑n≥1zn/ns\textrm{Li}_{s}(z)=\sum_{n\geq 1}z^{n}/n^{s} for s∈ℕ⋆s\in\mathbb{N}^{\star}), and exp⁡(z)=∑n≥0zn/n!\exp(z)=\sum_{n\geq 0}z^{n}/n! are transcendental. However, when f⁡(z)f(z) is not given in closed form, but rather like in Stanley’s problem (S), by a linear differential equation with sufficiently many initial conditions, then Eisenstein’s criterion is difficult to apply. The main reason for this is a quite fundamental one: it is currently not known (and it is considered to be a difficult open problem) how to recognize that a P-recursive sequence (an)n(a_{n})_{n} given by a linear recurrence and initial conditions has integer terms (or, that it has almost integer coefficients, in the sense that an​Cna_{n}C^{n} are integers for all n≥1n\geq 1, for some constant C∈ℕ∗C\in\mathbb{N}^{*}). The same difficulty arises in a different context for the mere problem of representing EE-functions, see [18].

1.4.2. Flajolet’s criterion

In many situations, the given D-finite power series f⁡(z)f(z) already has integer coefficients, therefore Eisenstein’s criterion is useless. This is systematically the case in combinatorics when f⁡(z)f(z) is the generating function of a sequence whose nnth term counts the number of objects of size nn in some combinatorial class. Much more useful is Flajolet’s criterion [38, Criterion D] (see also [39, VII.7.2]) based on the Newton-Puiseux theorem and on Darboux’s transfer results from the local behavior of f⁡(z)f(z) around its complex singularities to the asymptotic behavior of its coefficient sequence (an)n≥0(a_{n})_{n\geq 0}.

One form of the criterion asserts that if an∼γ​βn​nra_{n}\sim\gamma\,\beta^{n}\,n^{r} as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty, with either rr an irrational number or a negative integer, or β\beta a transcendental number, or γ⋅Γ⁡(r+1)\gamma\cdot\Gamma(r+1) a transcendental number, then f⁡(z)f(z) is transcendental.

For more general and more refined versions on the asymptotic behavior of the coefficients of algebraic power series, we refer to [39, p. 501], [82] and [90, Theorem 3.1].

This criterion is the most commonly used for transcendence questions in combinatorics. It allows for instance to show that if k∈ℕ⋆k\in\mathbb{N}^{\star}, then the hypergeometric power series ∑n≥0(2​nn)k​zn\sum_{n\geq 0}\binom{2n}{n}^{k}z^{n} (mentioned at the end of problem (g) in [103, §4]) is algebraic if and only if k=1k=1 (see Section 1.6 for a different proof), and also that the non-hypergeometric power series ∑n≥0∑k=0n(nk)2​(n+kk)2​zn\sum_{n\geq 0}\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}^{2}\binom{n+k}{k}^{2}z^{n} (occurring in Apéry’s celebrated proof of the irrationality of ζ⁡(3)\zeta(3), see Example 5) is transcendental. A more general example that can be handled by Flajolet’s criterion is

∑n≥0(∑k=0n(nk)p0​(n+kk)p1​(n+2​kk)p2​⋯​(n+m​kk)pm)​zn,\sum_{n\geq 0}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}^{p_{0}}\binom{n+k}{k}^{p_{1}}\binom{n+2k}{k}^{p_{2}}\dotsm\binom{n+mk}{k}^{p_{m}}\right)z^{n},

with pi∈ℕp_{i}\in\mathbb{N}, that is discussed in Appendix A.

However, there are cases of D-finite power series f⁡(z)f(z) for which both Eisenstein’s criterion and Flajolet’s criterion fail to detect the transcendence of f⁡(z)f(z), see Example 6.

1.5. A bit of history

Since the beginning of the 19th century, many works have been dedicated to solving problems (F) and (L), using various tools, from geometry (Schwarz, Klein), to invariants (Fuchs, Gordan) and from group theory (Jordan) to differential Galois theory (Kolchin, Singer).

Already in 1833, Liouville [73] proposed an algorithm for computing a basis of rational solutions (that is, solutions in ℚ⁡(z)\mathbb{Q}(z)) of linear differential equations like (1). This algorithm (with some enhancements and improvements, e.g., [1]) is the one currently implemented in most computer algebra systems. Liouville’s algorithm clearly solves the variants (F)rat{}_{\text{rat}} and (L)rat{}_{\text{rat}} of problems (F) and (L), in which the word “algebraic” is replaced by “rational”; it can also be used to solve the variant (S)rat{}_{\text{rat}} of problem (S): from a basis of solutions r1​(z),…,rs​(z)r_{1}(z),\ldots,r_{s}(z) in ℚ⁡(z){\mathbb{Q}}(z) of LL, one first computes the right factor LratL^{\textrm{rat}} of LL whose solution space is spanned by the rational solutions of LL, as the LCLM66 6 We denote by LCLM​{L1,…,Lk}\text{LCLM}\{L_{1},\ldots,L_{k}\} the least common left multiple of the operators L1,…,LkL_{1},\ldots,L_{k}, that is the monic minimal order operator whose solution space contains the solution spaces of all LiL_{i}’s. of the differential operators ∂z−rj′(z)/rj(z)\partial_{z}-r_{j}^{\prime}(z)/r_{j}(z), and then one checks whether Lrat​(f)L^{\textrm{rat}}(f) is zero or not (using [18, Lemma 2.1]).

In 1839 Liouville addressed in [74] what we call problem (L). He partially solved it for second-order differential operators. For instance, he showed that the equation y′′+r⁡(z)​y=0y^{\prime\prime}+r(z)y=0 does not admit any nontrivial algebraic solution when r⁡(z)∈ℚ⁡[z]∖{0}r(z)\in{\mathbb{Q}}[z]\setminus\{0\}. (In particular, this holds for Airy’s equation y′′=z​yy^{\prime\prime}=zy.) One year later he proved the same for r⁡(z)=(1+z2)2/(2​z−2​z3)2r(z)=(1+z^{2})^{2}/(2z-2z^{3})^{2}, from which he deduced that the complete elliptic integral f⁡(z)=∫01𝑑x/(1−x2)​(1−z2​x2)f(z)=\int_{0}^{1}dx/\sqrt{(1-x^{2})(1-z^{2}x^{2})} is not algebraic (and not even Liouvillian, that is, solvable in terms of integrals, exponentials and algebraic functions). In 1841, he applied his method to the Bessel equation z2​f′′​(z)+z​f′​(z)+(z2−μ2)​f​(z)=0z^{2}f^{\prime\prime}(z)+zf^{\prime}(z)+(z^{2}-\mu^{2})f(z)=0. However, he could not solve the problem when r⁡(z)r(z) is an arbitrary rational function; he reduced it to upper bounding the possible algebraicity degree of a solution. With such a bound BB at hand, Liouville reduced problem (L) to finding rational solutions of the symmetric powers L○s​mL^{{\scriptstyle\bigcirc\hskip-6.544pt\raisebox{0.5123pt}{${\scriptstyle s}$}}\hskip 2.84544ptm} (that is the monic minimal order operator whose solution space contains the powers fmf^{m} for all solutions ff of LL) for 1≤m≤B1\leq m\leq B.

Liouville’s work was taken up by Pépin (1863, 1878, 1881), who focused on problem (F) and managed to remove the restriction on the algebraicity degree [84, 85]. His 1863 paper contained a few errors corrected in 1878 (after remarks by Fuchs). Pépin completed his study in his long memoir published in 1881 [83]; there, he proved that if the equation y′′+r⁡(z)​y=0y^{\prime\prime}+r(z)y=0 has algebraic solutions only, then it admits a basis of solutions {y1,y2}\{y_{1},y_{2}\} such that either (i)(i) y1=amy_{1}=\sqrt[m]{a} and y2=b/y1y_{2}=b/y_{1}, for a,ba,b in ℚ⁡(z){\mathbb{Q}}(z) and m∈ℕ⋆m\in{\mathbb{N}}^{\star}; or (i​i)(ii) yimy_{i}^{m} are both roots of a quadratic equation over ℚ⁡(z){\mathbb{Q}}(z) for m∈ℕ⋆m\in{\mathbb{N}}^{\star}; or (i​i​i)(iii) yimy_{i}^{m} are both roots of an equation of degree μ\mu over ℚ⁡(z){\mathbb{Q}}(z), where (m,μ)∈{(4,6),(6,8),(12,10)}(m,\mu)\in\{(4,6),(6,8),(12,10)\}. In all cases, yi′/yiy_{i}^{\prime}/y_{i} is algebraic of degree 1, 2, 4, 6 or 12.

Meanwhile, in 1873, Schwarz [95] famously solved problem (F) for second-order operators with three singular points (the Gauss hypergeometric equation), see Section 1.6. Fuchs showed in 1876 that if y′′+r⁡(z)​y=0y^{\prime\prime}+r(z)y=0 has a nontrivial algebraic solution, then there exists a binary homogeneous form FF of degree d≤12d\leq 12 such that, for some basis {y1,y2}\{y_{1},y_{2}\} of solutions, F⁡(y1,y2)F(y_{1},y_{2}) is the kk-th root of a rational function for some explicit number kk depending only on dd. Inspired by Fuchs’s work, Klein showed in 1877 that any second-order linear differential equation with only algebraic solutions comes from some hypergeometric equation from Schwarz’s list via a rational change of variables. In [5], Dwork and Baldassarri discuss Klein’s and Fuchs’s articles and make Klein’s approach algorithmic. Sanabria Malagón generalizes this approach in [92], where he also gives a history of the evolution of this approach through his work and that of others. Another approach was proposed by Jordan (1878) who showed that if all solutions of (1) are algebraic, then there exists a solution whose logarithmic derivative is algebraic of degree at most J⁡(r)J(r), an explicit number depending only on the order rr. Jordan’s article and the works by Painlevé (1887) and his student Boulanger (1898) are the starting points of modern algorithms by Singer [96, 97], who completely solved problem (F), see Section 1.7. References to improvements on this algorithm are given in [100].

For more historical aspects related to these rich problems, we refer the interested reader to the following sources: [19, p. 1–13], [108, p. 160–165], [44, p. 5–10], [75, p. 407–413], [98, p. 25], [100, p. 533–536], [107, p. 124] and [45, p. 48–50, 273–274, and Chap. III].

1.6. The hypergeometric case

A very particular, yet quite important special case of D-finite power series f∈ℚ⁡[[z]]f\in{\mathbb{Q}}[[z]] is the hypergeometric class. This means that the coefficient sequence of f⁡(z)f(z) satisfies a first-order homogeneous linear recurrence with polynomial coefficients. Typical examples are log⁡(1−z)\log(1-z), arcsin⁡(z)/z{\arcsin(\sqrt{z})}/{\sqrt{z}}, (1−z)α{(1-z)^{\alpha}} for α∈ℚ\alpha\in{\mathbb{Q}}, and more generally the Gaussian hypergeometric function with parameters a,b,c∈ℚa,b,c\in{\mathbb{Q}} (−c∉ℕ-c\notin{\mathbb{N}}),

F12[a​bc;z]≔∑n=0∞(a)n​(b)n(c)nznn!,where(d)n≔d(d+1)⋯(d+n−1),{{}_{2}F_{1}\biggl[\begin{matrix}{a\ b}\\ {c}\end{matrix}\,;\,z\biggr]\coloneq\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a)_{n}(b)_{n}}{(c)_{n}}\,\frac{z^{n}}{n!},\quad\text{where}\quad(d)_{n}\coloneq d(d+1)\cdots(d+n-1),}

solution of the differential equation z⁡(1−z)​f′′​(z)+(c−(a+b+1)​z)​f′​(z)−a​b​f​(z)=0z(1-z)f^{\prime\prime}(z)+(c-(a+b+1)z)f^{\prime}(z)-abf(z)=0.

Deciding the algebraicity of F12{}_{2}F_{1} functions is an old problem, first solved by Schwarz [95] using geometric and complex analytic tools, and later by Landau [69, 70] and Errera [36] using number theoretic tools. Both approaches are algorithmic: Schwarz’s criterion reduces the problem to a table look-up after some preprocessing on the parameters a,b,ca,b,c; the Landau-Errera criterion amounts to checking a finite number of inequalities. The reader is referred to [12, §2.1.3] and to Matsuda’s book [76, Chap. I, II and IV] for more details.

The definition of the Gaussian hypergeometric function extends to the generalized hypergeometric function with complex parameters aia_{i} and bib_{i} with −bi∉ℕ-b_{i}\not\in\mathbb{N}

Fℓk​[a1a2⋯akb1⋯bℓ;z]≔∑n=0∞(a1)n⋯(ak)n(b1)n⋯(bℓ)n​znn!.{{}_{k}F_{\ell}}\biggl[\begin{matrix}{a_{1}}\kern 7.07pt{a_{2}}\kern 7.07pt{\cdots}\kern 7.07pt{a_{k}}\\ {b_{1}}\kern 7.07pt{\cdots}\kern 7.07pt{b_{\ell}}\end{matrix}\,;\,z\biggr]\coloneq\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a_{1})_{n}\cdots(a_{k})_{n}}{(b_{1})_{n}\cdots(b_{\ell})_{n}}\,\frac{z^{n}}{n!}.

When ℓ≠k−1\ell\neq k-1, a Fℓk{}_{k}F_{\ell} non-polynomial hypergeometric function in ℚ⁡[[z]]\mathbb{Q}[[z]] cannot be algebraic, by Stirling’s formula combined with Flajolet’s criterion; alternatively, because for k>ℓ+1k>\ell+1 the power series Fℓk{}_{k}F_{\ell} has radius of convergence 0, while Fℓk{}_{k}F_{\ell} is an entire function for k≤ℓk\leq\ell.

When ℓ=k−1\ell=k-1 and the parameters are rational numbers, the Landau-Errera criterion was extended by Christol [23, §VI] under a conjecture, and by Beukers and Heckman [8] unconditionally. To state it, we need the following definitions: for x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} we denote by ⟨x⟩\langle x\rangle its fractional part x−⌊x⌋x-\lfloor x\rfloor if x∉ℤx\notin{\mathbb{Z}}, and 1 if x∈ℤx\in{\mathbb{Z}}; we say that two equinumerous disjoint multisets of real numbers {u1,…,uk}\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{k}\} and {v1,…,vk}\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{k}\} with ⟨u1⟩≤⋯≤⟨uk⟩\langle u_{1}\rangle\leq\cdots\leq\langle u_{k}\rangle and ⟨v1⟩≤⋯≤⟨vk⟩\langle v_{1}\rangle\leq\cdots\leq\langle v_{k}\rangle interlace if ⟨u1⟩<⟨v1⟩<⋯<⟨uk⟩<⟨vk⟩\langle u_{1}\rangle<\langle v_{1}\rangle<\cdots<\langle u_{k}\rangle<\langle v_{k}\rangle. Now, let 𝐚={a1,…,ak}⊂ℚ{\bf a}=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}\}\subset{\mathbb{Q}} and 𝐛={b1,…,bk−1,bk=1}⊂ℚ∖(−ℕ){\bf b}=\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{k-1},b_{k}=1\}\subset{\mathbb{Q}}\setminus(-{\mathbb{N}}) be two multisets of rational parameters assumed to be disjoint modulo ℤ\mathbb{Z}. This assumption is equivalent to the irreducibility of the generalized hypergeometric operator H𝐛𝐚≔(z∂z+b1−1)⋯(z∂z+bk−1−1)z∂z−z(z∂z+a1)⋯(z∂z+ak)H_{\bf b}^{\bf a}\coloneq(z\partial_{z}+b_{1}-1)\cdots(z\partial_{z}+b_{k-1}-1)z\partial_{z}-z(z\partial_{z}+a_{1})\cdots(z\partial_{z}+a_{k}). Let DD be the common denominator of a1,…,ak,b1,…,bk−1a_{1},\ldots,a_{k},b_{1},\ldots,b_{k-1}. Then, the function Fk−1k{}_{k}F_{k-1} is a solution of H𝐛𝐚H_{\bf b}^{\bf a} and the interlacing criterion says that it is algebraic if and only if for all 1≤ℓ<D1\leq\ell<D with gcd⁡(ℓ,D)=1\gcd(\ell,D)=1 the multisets ℓ​𝐚\ell{\bf a} and ℓ​𝐛\ell{\bf b} interlace (pictorially, this means that the points {e2​π​i​ℓ​aj,j≤k}\{e^{2\pi i\ell a_{j}},j\leq k\} and {e2​π​i​ℓ​bj,j≤k}\{e^{2\pi i\ell b_{j}},j\leq k\} interlace on the unit circle).

For instance, the Beukers-Heckman criterion immediately implies that the power series

∑n=0∞(2​nn)k​zn=Fk−1k​[1212⋯121⋯1; 4k​z]\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\binom{2n}{n}^{\!k}z^{n}={{}_{k}F_{k-1}}\biggl[\begin{matrix}{\frac{1}{2}}\kern 7.07pt{\frac{1}{2}}\kern 7.07pt{\cdots}\kern 7.07pt{\frac{1}{2}}\\ {1}\kern 7.07pt{\cdots}\kern 7.07pt{1}\end{matrix}\,;\,4^{k}\,z\biggr]

is transcendental for all k≥2k\geq 2, since the interlacing condition is violated. This example is mentioned by Stanley in [103, §4, (g)] as one of the motivations of his general question (S).

The Beukers-Heckman interlacing criterion does not cover all cases of hypergeometric functions in ℚ⁡[[z]]\mathbb{Q}[[z]]; it cannot be used if some parameters are irrational nor if a difference between a top and a bottom parameter is an integer. For this reason, the following examples escape it

(2) F12​[1 12;z],F12​[2 21;z]andF23​[1/2​1+2​1−22−2;z].{}_{2}F_{1}\biggl[\begin{matrix}{1\ 1}\\ {2}\end{matrix}\,;\,z\biggr],\quad{}_{2}F_{1}\biggl[\begin{matrix}{2\ 2}\\ {1}\end{matrix}\,;\,z\biggr]\quad\text{and}\quad{{}_{3}F_{2}}\biggl[\begin{matrix}{1/2}\kern 7.07pt{1+\sqrt{2}}\kern 7.07pt{1-\sqrt{2}}\\ {\sqrt{2}}\kern 7.07pt{-\sqrt{2}}\end{matrix}\,;\,z\biggr].

Fürnsinn and Yurkevich [41] provided a complete classification of the algebraic generalized hypergeometric functions with no restriction on the set of their parameters, thus answering completely Stanley’s question (S) for power series whose coefficient sequences satisfy a recurrence of order 1. Their result is algorithmic and makes it possible to prove that, among the three examples in Eq. 2, the first power series is transcendental, while the last two are algebraic. Their algorithm relies on an ingenious, albeit elementary, reduction of the general case to the interlacing criterion of Beukers and Heckman [41, Fig. 1].

1.7. Singer’s algorithm for problem (F)

In the 1980s, Michael Singer [96, 97] designed algorithms that solve Fuchs’ problem (F). In fact, the problem had essentially been solved in the second half of the 19th century, for order 2 equations by Schwarz, Klein, Fuchs, and for order 3 equations by Painlevé and Boulanger. For an irreducible operator LL of order rr, Singer’s algorithm in [96] relies on differential Galois theory and proceeds in two main steps:

  1. (i)

    (Jordan’s bound) decide if the (nonlinear) Riccati differential equation77 7 By definition, RLR_{L} has order r−1r-1 and has the property that ff is a nonzero solution of LL if and only if f′/ff^{\prime}/f is a solution of RLR_{L}. RL​(u)=0R_{L}(u)=0 attached to LL admits an algebraic solution uu of degree at most (49​r)r2(49r)^{r^{2}};

  2. (ii)

    (Abel’s problem) given an algebraic uu, decide whether y′/y=uy^{\prime}/y=u admits an algebraic solution yy.

Step (ii) is solved by Risch’s algorithm [89] (and independently by Baldassarri and Dwork [5, §6]); it was the missing ingredient in the 19th century procedures. Singer solves Step (i) by reducing it to an algebraic elimination problem. Part of the proof of the algorithm is that if step (ii) finds an algebraic yy such that y′/y=uy^{\prime}/y=u with uu as in step (i), then yy is a nontrivial algebraic solution of LL, and since LL is irreducible, all solutions of LL are algebraic.

In the reducible case, Singer’s algorithm first proceeds with a factorization step that writes LL as a product of irreducible operators. The corresponding detailed results and procedures can be found in (the proofs of) [96, Theorem 1] in the irreducible case, and [96, Theorem 3] in the general case. A slightly different route is proposed by Singer in [97, Corollary 4.3], where first a basis of all Liouvillian solutions is computed, and then an algorithm by Rothstein and Caviness [91, §4] is used to decide if all elements in this basis are algebraic.

1.8. Other approaches to problem (F)

Another way of seeing that Fuchs’ problem (F) is decidable, in a spirit similar to Singer’s algorithm but of even higher algorithmic complexity, is based on the equivalence for a linear differential operator LL between having a full basis of algebraic solutions and having a finite differential Galois group. Indeed, since Hrushovski’s seminal article [58], it is known that one can fully determine algorithmically the Galois group of LL. (Prior to  [58], it was only known how to compute the Galois group of completely reducible operators, that is for operators LL that can be written as LCLM of irreducible operators [28], a condition that can itself be algorithmically tested [99].) The complexity of Hrushovski’s algorithm is not yet fully understood, and its simplification is the object of ongoing works, e.g., [37, 105, 2]. An approach to understanding the Galois group of LL by computing the Lie algebra of its identity component is given in [6, 7] and [33]. In a different direction, van der Hoeven proposed in [55] a symbolic-numeric approach for computing differential Galois groups, but for the moment its potential has not been exploited further.

To our knowledge, none of the algorithms mentioned in Sections 1.7 and 1.8 has been implemented yet, nor are they expected to provide good practical behavior (except perhaps for very moderate orders, as in e.g., [101, 54]).

Let us finally mention a very recent sufficient (algorithmic) criterion for problem (𝐅){\bf(F)}. Assume that the linear differential equation L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0 admits a basis of Puiseux series solutions at each of its singularities. Assume moreover that there exists another differential operator PP such that ∂zP\partial_{z}P is not right-divisible by LL and such that for all singularities σ\sigma of LL and for all elements ff in a basis of Puiseux solutions of LL at σ\sigma, the Puiseux series P⁡(f)P(f) has only nonnegative exponents. Then LL admits a transcendental solution, in other words Fuchs’ problem (𝐅){\bf(F)} is answered by the negative. This is the content of [62, Thm. 5], where such an operator PP is called a pseudoconstant. Moreover, Algorithm 10 in [62] is able to compute a pseudoconstant for LL, or to certify that none exists. More generally, if any symmetric power of LL admits a pseudoconstant, then LL admits a transcendental solution (Theorem 18 in [62]). Conversely, it is an open question whether the fact that LL admits transcendental solutions implies the existence of pseudoconstants for some symmetric power of LL [62, Question 20]. If the answer to this open question were positive, then this would provide another way to show that Fuchs’ problem is decidable.

2. Solving problem (S)

For a D-finite power series f∈ℚ⁡[[z]]f\in{\mathbb{Q}}[[z]], we write LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} for the monic linear differential operator in ℚ(z)⟨∂z⟩{\mathbb{Q}}(z)\langle\partial_{z}\rangle of minimal order that annihilates ff. By a slight abuse of notation, we sometimes write LfminL^{\text{min}}_{f} for the operator in ℚ[z]⟨∂z⟩{\mathbb{Q}}[z]\langle\partial_{z}\rangle of the same order, obtained by clearing denominators. These two operators differ by a multiplicative factor in ℚ⁡(z){\mathbb{Q}}(z). Both operators have the same main properties (solution space, local bases, singularities, …). The degree of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} is the maximal degree of its coefficients in the second representation. LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} can be computed efficiently [18] starting from any linear differential equation satisfied by ff together with sufficiently many initial terms of ff.

Our solution to Stanley’s problem (S) is based on the properties of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} that we review now.

2.1. Properties of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f}

In simple terms, the minimal differential operator LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} is a differential analogue for D-finite functions of the more classical notion of minimal polynomial for algebraic power series. Indeed, any L∈ℚ[z]⟨∂z⟩L\in{\mathbb{Q}}[z]\langle\partial_{z}\rangle such that L⁡(f⁡(z))=0L(f(z))=0 is a left multiple of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} in the ring ℚ(z)⟨∂z⟩{\mathbb{Q}}(z)\langle\partial_{z}\rangle, and conversely any left multiple of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} is an annihilator for ff.

But there are two main differences between these similar notions. One is that, for such an LL, although its order upper bounds the order of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f}, it is in general not the case that the maximal degree of the coefficients of LL is an upper bound on the maximal degree of the coefficients of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f}; this is actually the main difficulty in the algorithmic computation of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f}, see [18] for more details. Another difference important to note is that LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} does not need to be irreducible in ℚ(z)⟨∂z⟩{\mathbb{Q}}(z)\langle\partial_{z}\rangle. Reducibility can already occur when ff is transcendental, as illustrated by Llog⁡(1−z)min=((1−z)∂z−1)∂zL^{\mathrm{min}}_{\log(1-z)}=((1-z)\partial_{z}-1)\partial_{z}. The same also holds when ff is algebraic. For instance, for the algebraic power series of degree 2

f=1−4​z+z=1−z−2​z2−4​z3−10​z4−⋯,f=\sqrt{1-4z}+z=1-z-2z^{2}-4z^{3}-10z^{4}-\cdots,

we have that

Lminf=(1−2z)(1−4z)∂z2−4z∂z+4=((1−2z)(1−4z)∂z+4z−6+1z)⋅(∂z−1z).L^{\mathrm{min}}_{f}=\left(1-2z\right)\left(1-4z\right)\partial_{z}^{2}-4z\partial_{z}+4\\ =\left(\left(1-2z\right)\left(1-4z\right)\partial_{z}+4z-6+\frac{1}{z}\right)\cdot\left(\partial_{z}-\frac{1}{z}\right).

Moreover, this is actually the “generic behavior” for an algebraic power series f∈ℚ⁡[[z]]f\in{\mathbb{Q}}[[z]]: if P=yd+cd−1​(z)​yd−1+⋯+c0​(z)=∏ℓ=1d(y−fℓ​(z))P=y^{d}+c_{d-1}(z)y^{d-1}+\cdots+c_{0}(z)=\prod_{\ell=1}^{d}(y-f_{\ell}(z)) is the minimal polynomial of f=f1f=f_{1} in ℚ​(z)​[y]{\mathbb{Q}}(z)[y], then LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} annihilates all the conjugate roots f2,…,fdf_{2},\ldots,f_{d} of f=f1f=f_{1} (see Proposition 3). Therefore, LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} admits ∑ℓ=1dfℓ​(z)=−cd−1​(z)\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}f_{\ell}(z)=-c_{d-1}(z) as rational solution, hence if cd−1≠0c_{d-1}\neq 0 then LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} is right-divisible by ∂z−cd−1′/cd−1\partial_{z}-c_{d-1}^{\prime}/c_{d-1}. This was remarked by Tannery [106, p. 132], see also [29, Prop. 4.2].

In Proposition 3 below we give properties of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} and related operators. The proofs rely on some basic facts from the Galois theory of linear differential equations (see [98, 107]), so we begin in this general setting. Let kk be a differential field of characteristic zero with derivation ∂\partial and whose field of constants C={c∈k|∂c=0}C=\{c\in k\ |\ \partial c=0\} is algebraically closed. Let L∈k⟨∂⟩L\in k\langle\partial\rangle be an operator of order rr and let KK be the associated Picard-Vessiot extension88 8 This is a field generated over kk by a fundamental set of solutions and all their derivatives through order r−1r-1 and having the same constants CC as kk; one sees that it is again a differential field. Since we assume that CC is algebraically closed, such a field exists and any two are differentially isomorphic over kk.. Let GG be the differential Galois group of KK over kk and let f∈Kf\in K be a solution of L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0. We define LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} to be the monic operator in k⟨∂⟩k\langle\partial\rangle of smallest order vanishing on ff99 9 This definition is reconciled with the previous one before Proposition 3..

The CC-space of algebraic solutions of L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0 is left invariant by the action of GG, so it is the solution space of a monic operator in k⟨∂⟩k\langle\partial\rangle denoted by LalgL^{\mathrm{alg}} ([99, Lemma 2.2] or [107, Lemma 2.17 p. 48])00footnotemark: 0 . Let P⁡(Y)P(Y) be an irreducible polynomial in k⁡[Y]k[Y] and assume that there is a u∈Ku\in K such that P⁡(u)=0P(u)=0. The differential Galois theory implies that the splitting field of PP over kk lies in KK [107, Prop. 1.34.3]. Since GG permutes the roots of P⁡(Y)P(Y), we have that the CC-span of these roots is left invariant under this action. As before, this implies that this vector space is the solution space of a monic operator in k⟨∂⟩k\langle\partial\rangle, denoted by LPL_{P}. Note that since Picard-Vessiot extensions for LL are unique up to kk-differential isomorphisms, the operators Lalg,LfminL^{\mathrm{alg}},L^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} and LPL_{P} will be independent of such an extension since any such isomorphism will preserve all the properties of these operators.

We shall apply the above constructions to a linear differential operator L∈ℚ¯(z)⟨∂z⟩L\in{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(z)\langle\partial_{z}\rangle. To be precise, by an algebraic solution we mean an element y∈𝒫=⋃n∈ℕ⋆ℚ¯​((z1n))y\in{\mathcal{P}}=\bigcup_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{\star}}{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}((z^{\frac{1}{n}})), the differential field of formal Puiseux series where ∂z(z1n)=1n​z1n−1\partial_{z}(z^{\frac{1}{n}})=\frac{1}{n}z^{\frac{1}{n}-1} such that yy is algebraic over ℚ¯​(z){\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(z) and L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0. For a given operator LL, the set 𝒜L{\mathcal{A}}^{L} of algebraic solutions forms a vector space over ℚ¯{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}} of dimension at most r=ord⁡(L)r={\operatorname{ord}}(L). Furthermore, the derivation ∂z\partial_{z} extends uniquely to the field E=ℚ¯​(z,𝒜L)E={\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(z,{\mathcal{A}}^{L}). We now construct a Picard-Vessiot extension KK of k=ℚ¯​(z)k={\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(z) that contains 𝒜L{\mathcal{A}}^{L}. Let FF be the Picard-Vessiot extension of EE corresponding to LL. Since 𝒜L{\mathcal{A}}^{L} lies in the solution space of LL in EE, there exists a basis {y1,…,yr}\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{r}\} of this space that contains a basis of 𝒜L{\mathcal{A}}^{L}. The field K=ℚ¯​(z)​(y1,…,yr,…,y1(r−1),…,yr(r−1))⊂FK={\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(z)(y_{1},\ldots,y_{r},\ldots,y_{1}^{(r-1)},\ldots,y_{r}^{(r-1)})\subset F has no new constants and so is the required Picard-Vessiot extension.

If both k=ℚ¯​(z)k={\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(z) and f∈ℚ⁡[[z]]f\in{\mathbb{Q}}[[z]], Proposition 3 below shows that LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} and LalgL^{\mathrm{alg}} have coefficients in ℚ⁡(z)\mathbb{Q}(z). Therefore in this special case, the definitions of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} and LalgL^{\mathrm{alg}} coincide with those given earlier.

Proposition 3.

Let L∈ℚ(z)⟨∂⟩L\in{\mathbb{Q}}(z)\langle\partial\rangle and f∈ℚ⁡[[z]]f\in{\mathbb{Q}}[[z]] be an algebraic solution of L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0 with minimal polynomial P​(Y)∈ℚ​(z)​[Y]P(Y)\in{\mathbb{Q}}(z)[Y]. If Lalg,LPL^{\mathrm{alg}},L_{P}, and LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} are the operators defined above over ℚ¯​(z){\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(z), then these operators have coefficients in ℚ⁡(z){\mathbb{Q}}(z). Furthermore, Lfmin=LPL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f}=L_{P} so the solution space of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} is spanned by the roots of P⁡(Y)P(Y). In particular, the local solutions of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} at any of its singularities do not contain logarithms.

Proof.

Once again let 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} be the differential field of Puiseux series and let Gal⁡(ℚ¯/ℚ)\operatorname{Gal}({\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}/{\mathbb{Q}}) be the Galois group of ℚ¯{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}} over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}. For σ∈Gal⁡(ℚ¯/ℚ)\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}({\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}/{\mathbb{Q}}), we define the action of σ\sigma on 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} as σ⁡(∑iai​zin)=∑iσ⁡(ai)​zin\sigma(\sum_{i}a_{i}z^{\frac{i}{n}})=\sum_{i}\sigma(a_{i})z^{\frac{i}{n}}. In this way Gal⁡(ℚ¯/ℚ)\operatorname{Gal}({\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}/{\mathbb{Q}}) acts on 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} as a group of differential automorphisms with fixed field ⋃n∈ℕ⋆ℚ⁡((z1n))\bigcup_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{\star}}{\mathbb{Q}}((z^{\frac{1}{n}})).

𝑳𝐚𝐥𝐠\boldsymbol{L^{\mathrm{alg}}}: Since LL has coefficients in ℚ⁡(z){\mathbb{Q}}(z), Gal⁡(ℚ¯/ℚ)\operatorname{Gal}({\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}/{\mathbb{Q}}) leaves the ℚ¯{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}-space of algebraic solutions invariant. Denoting by σ​Lalg\sigma L^{\mathrm{alg}} the operator obtained from LalgL^{\mathrm{alg}} by applying σ\sigma to the coefficients of LalgL^{\mathrm{alg}}, we have that σ​Lalg\sigma L^{\mathrm{alg}} and LalgL^{\mathrm{alg}} have the same solution spaces and so must be equal. Therefore LalgL^{\mathrm{alg}} has coefficients in ℚ⁡(z){\mathbb{Q}}(z).

𝑳𝑷\boldsymbol{L_{P}}: Since P⁡(Y)P(Y) has coefficients in ℚ⁡(z){\mathbb{Q}}(z), Gal⁡(ℚ¯/ℚ)\operatorname{Gal}({\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}/{\mathbb{Q}}) permutes its roots and therefore the ℚ¯{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}-space spanned by these roots is left invariant by this action. Arguing as above we have that LPL_{P} has coefficients in ℚ⁡(z){\mathbb{Q}}(z).

𝑳𝒇𝐦𝐢𝐧\boldsymbol{L^{\mathrm{min}}_{f}}: Any σ∈Gal⁡(ℚ¯/ℚ)\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}({\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}/{\mathbb{Q}}) leaves ff fixed and sends LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} to σ​Lfmin\sigma L^{\mathrm{min}}_{f}. By uniqueness of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f}, we have Lfmin=σ​LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f}=\sigma L^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} and this implies, as above, that the coefficients of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} lie in ℚ⁡(z){\mathbb{Q}}(z).

𝑳𝒇𝐦𝐢𝐧=𝑳𝑷\boldsymbol{L^{\mathrm{min}}_{f}}\boldsymbol{=}\boldsymbol{L_{P}}: Let FF be the splitting field of P⁡(Y)P(Y) over ℚ⁡(z){\mathbb{Q}}(z) and let HH be the (usual) Galois group of this extension. The derivation on ℚ⁡(z){\mathbb{Q}}(z) extends uniquely to a derivation on FF and the elements of HH commute with this derivation. Since P⁡(Y)P(Y) is irreducible, HH acts transitively on the roots of P⁡(Y)P(Y). Since LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} has coefficients in ℚ⁡(z){\mathbb{Q}}(z) and vanishes on one root of P⁡(Y)P(Y), LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} vanishes on all the roots and therefore on the ℚ¯{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}-space spanned by the roots of P⁡(Y)P(Y). This implies that LPL_{P} is a right factor of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f}. Minimality of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} and the fact that LP​(f)=0L_{P}(f)=0 implies that LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} is a right factor of LPL_{P}. Therefore these two operators are equal.

Finally, the local branches of the roots of PP are Puiseux series at every finite point and at infinity. Since these roots span the solution space of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f}, it admits at every point a local fundamental system of Puiseux solutions and therefore no logarithmic local solutions. ∎

Proposition 3 implies the following classical result (for definitions of the terms see [59, Chap. 15-16]):

Corollary 4.

The differential operator LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} of an algebraic power series f∈ℚ⁡[[z]]f\in{\mathbb{Q}}[[z]] enjoys the following properties:

  1. (1)

    it is Fuchsian;

  2. (2)

    it admits only rational exponents at all its singular points;

  3. (3)

    the monic indicial polynomials at all of its singular points split in ℚ⁡[z]{\mathbb{Q}}[z] into distinct linear factors.

Proof.

By Proposition 3, all solutions of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} are algebraic. Fuchs proved that in this situation, the differential operator satisfies properties (1) and (2) [40, §6.II]. Conclusion (3) is a consequence of the fact that a multiple root of the indicial equation at z=az=a always introduces logarithmic terms in the basis of local solutions at z=az=a [40, §6.I], see also [59, p. 405]. ∎

This recurrence is then converted into a linear differential equation L⁡(f)=0L(f)=0 satisfied by f⁡(z)f(z), where LL is the differential operator

L=(z4−34z3+z2)∂z3+(6z3−153z2+3z)∂z2+(7z2−112z+1)∂z+z−5.L=(z^{4}-34z^{3}+z^{2})\partial_{z}^{3}+(6z^{3}-153z^{2}+3z)\partial_{z}^{2}+(7z^{2}-112z+1)\partial_{z}+z-5.

In the third step one certifies that Lfmin=LL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f}=L, meaning that LL is already the minimal-order differential equation satisfied by f⁡(z)f(z). This can be done using the minimization procedure in [18, Algorithm 1]1010 10 Note that in this very particular case, one could alternatively prove that LL is actually irreducible (for instance, by showing that neither LL, nor its adjoint, admit any non-trivial hyperexponential solutions)..

Finally, the indicial polynomial of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} at z=0z=0 is z3z^{3}, and the transcendence of f⁡(z)f(z) follows from part (3) of Corollary 4.

The approach used in Example 5 is the basis of Algorithms 2 and 3 below.

Note that there are alternative proofs for the transcendence of the Apéry series f⁡(z)f(z). One of them relies on the combination of three (non-trivial) ingredients: (i) the asymptotics An∼(1+2)4​n+229/4​π3/2​n3/2A_{n}\sim\frac{(1+\sqrt{2})^{4n+2}}{2^{9/4}\pi^{3/2}n^{3/2}} [78]; (ii) Flajolet’s criterion (Section 1.4.2); (iii) the fact that π\pi is transcendental. Our proof based on differential operators appears to be more “natural”, since proving the transcendence of a function should be easier than proving the transcendence of a number. Another alternative proof uses [22, Thm. 5.1] (see also [113, §6]); it relies on the fact that f⁡(z)f(z) admits modular parametrizations, implying that, up to an algebraic transformation, f⁡(z)f(z) coincides with the hypergeometric series F23​[1/2​1/2​1/21​1;z]{{}_{3}F_{2}}\biggl[\begin{matrix}{1/2}\kern 7.07pt{1/2}\kern 7.07pt{1/2}\\ {1}\kern 7.07pt{1}\end{matrix}\,;\,z\biggr], which is transcendental ( Section 1.6). This proof does not extend to more general Apéry-like series, such as those in Appendix A.

The next example is of a more combinatorial flavor. It exhibits a case of a nontrivial D-finite power series f⁡(z)f(z) in ℚ⁡[[z]]{\mathbb{Q}}[[z]] whose minimal-order operator LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} is not only reducible, but (almost) split.

Example 6.

The generating function of the “trident walks in the quarter plane” is the power series

f⁡(z)=∑n≥0an​zn=1+2​z+7​z2+23​z3+84​z4+301​z5+1127​z6+⋯.f(z)=\sum_{n\geq 0}a_{n}z^{n}=1+2\,z+7\,z^{2}+23\,z^{3}+84\,z^{4}+301\,z^{5}+1127\,z^{6}+\cdots.

Its nnth coefficient ana_{n} counts all the -walks of length nn in ℕ2{\mathbb{N}}^{2} starting at (0,0)(0,0). It was proved in [15] that f⁡(z)f(z) satisfies L⁡(f)=0L(f)=0, where LL is a linear differential operator of order 5 and degree at most 15. In [15, §4.2] it was shown that f⁡(z)f(z) is transcendental by exploiting the full factorization of LL. An alternative proof of the transcendence of ff (and actually of all 4×19−4=724\times 19-4=72 similar power series in [15, Thm. 2], see Section 5) uses minimization to first prove that the differential equation L⁡(f)=0L(f)=0 has minimal order, that is Lfmin=LL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f}=L, and concludes using the presence of logarithmic terms in the local fundamental system of LL at z=0z=0. One advantage of this proof is that factorization of linear differential operators is avoided.

Flajolet’s asymptotic criterion used in the alternative proof for the Apéry series does not prove transcendence in Example 6. Indeed, the asymptotic behavior1111 11 This asymptotic estimate was conjectured in [15, Conjecture 1], shown to be equivalent to an integral evaluation in [15, Theorem 8], and proved using analytic combinatorics in several variables in [80, §6]. an∼γ​βn​nra_{n}\sim\gamma\beta^{n}n^{r} with γ=4/(3​π)\gamma=4/(3\sqrt{\pi}), β=4\beta=4, r=−1/2r=-1/2, is compatible with algebraicity, since r∈ℚ∖ℤ<0r\in{\mathbb{Q}}\setminus{\mathbb{Z}}_{<0}, β∈ℚ¯\beta\in{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}} and γ​Γ​(r+1)=4/3∈ℚ¯\gamma\Gamma(r+1)=4/3\in{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}.

Another combinatorial example, also arising from the world of lattice path enumeration, was considered in [11, Proposition 8.4]. In that case, all known criteria for transcendence fail to apply, as well as all previously known algorithms. Moreover, the defining differential operator (of order 11 and polynomial degree 73) could not be factored with the computer algebra systems of the time. The proof in [11, Proposition 8.4] relies on the computation of the corresponding minimal operator LfminL_{f}^{\text{min}}. This example was the starting point for Algorithms 1, 2 and 3.

2.3. An algorithm for Stanley’s problem (S)

Based on Proposition 3, a first solution to Stanley’s problem (S) is Algorithm 1. It solves it in principle, in the sense that it shows that (S) is decidable. However, its computational complexity is too high to be of practical use, mainly because it relies on the costly algorithm from [96].

Theorem 7.

Given a power series f∈ℚ⁡[[z]]f\in{\mathbb{Q}}[[z]] by a linear differential operator L∈ℚ[z]⟨∂z⟩L\in{\mathbb{Q}}[z]\langle\partial_{z}\rangle such that L⁡(f)=0L(f)=0, together with sufficiently many initial conditions, Algorithm 1 decides whether ff is algebraic or transcendental.

Proof.

If ff is algebraic then, by Proposition 3, LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} admits a full basis of algebraic solutions, and this is detected by Singer’s algorithm [96]. Conversely, if LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} admits a full basis of algebraic solutions then ff is a linear combination of the elements of this basis and therefore is algebraic. ∎

2.4. An efficient transcendence test

To go further towards a more efficient variant of Algorithm 1, we use Propositions 3 and 4.

Theorem 8.

Given a power series f∈ℚ⁡[[z]]f\in{\mathbb{Q}}[[z]] by a linear differential operator L∈ℚ[z]⟨∂z⟩L\in{\mathbb{Q}}[z]\langle\partial_{z}\rangle such that L⁡(f)=0L(f)=0, together with sufficiently many initial conditions, Algorithm 2 either proves that ff is transcendental or returns FAIL.

Proof.

Assume that ff is algebraic. By Corollary 4, LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} is Fuchsian and, at each of its singularities, its indicial polynomial has degree ord⁡(Lfmin){\operatorname{ord}}(L^{\mathrm{min}}_{f}) and has distinct rational roots. Therefore neither of the tests in lines 9 and 11 can return 𝖳\mathsf{T}.

Moreover, by Proposition 3, the local solutions of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} contain no logarithmic terms. Thus the logarithm test cannot return 𝖳\mathsf{T} either. Consequently, Algorithm 2 returns 𝖥𝖠𝖨𝖫\mathsf{FAIL} whenever ff is algebraic. Hence, whenever it returns 𝖳\mathsf{T}, the power series ff is transcendental. ∎

In terms of completeness, Algorithm 2 is not as good as Algorithm 1, since it does not detect algebraicity. As such, it is not a full decision procedure for transcendence. However, in terms of efficiency, Algorithm 2 is much better than Algorithm 1, as it only relies on the minimization algorithm from [18], plus a few computationally cheap local tests.

2.5. An efficient conditional algorithm in the globally bounded case

To state our next results, we now recall a collection of results and conjectures on D-finite globally bounded power series (see Definition 2). An important source of globally bounded power series is the class of diagonals of rational functions defined as follows.

Definition 9.

For a rational function R∈ℚ⁡(x1,…,xs)R\in\mathbb{Q}(x_{1},\dots,x_{s}) with Taylor expansion

∑i1≥0,…,is≥0ai1,…,is​x1i1​⋯​xsis\sum_{i_{1}\geq 0,\dots,i_{s}\geq 0}{a_{i_{1},\dots,i_{s}}x_{1}^{i_{1}}\dotsm x_{s}^{i_{s}}}

in the neighborhood of the origin, the diagonal Diag⁡(R){\operatorname{Diag}}(R) is the power series

Diag⁡(R)=∑i≥0ai,…,i​zi∈ℚ⁡[[z]].{\operatorname{Diag}}(R)=\sum_{i\geq 0}{a_{i,\dots,i}z^{i}}\in\mathbb{Q}[[z]].

A power series in ℚ⁡[[z]]\mathbb{Q}[[z]] is a diagonal of a rational function if it equals Diag⁡(R){\operatorname{Diag}}(R) for some rational function RR.

Algebraic functions are diagonals [42]. Diagonals of rational functions are D-finite and globally bounded [24, Proposition 5]. Moreover, a D-finite and globally bounded power series is a GG-function. A consequence is an extension of parts (1) and (2) of Corollary 4: LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} is Fuchsian with rational exponents at all its singular points. This follows from results of Katz (1970), Chudnovsky and Chudnovsky (1985) and André (1989), see e.g., [3, p. 719] or [72, Thm. 1] and the references therein1212 12 Note that part (3) of Corollary 4 is false for the larger class of diagonals, as the simple example f=Diag⁡(1/(1−(x1+x2)​(x3+1)))=∑n≥0(2​nn)2​znf={\operatorname{Diag}}\left({1}/(1-(x_{1}+x_{2})(x_{3}+1))\right)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\binom{2n}{n}^{2}z^{n} demonstrates, since Lfmin=(16z2−z)∂z2+(32z−1)∂z+4L^{\mathrm{min}}_{f}=\left(16z^{2}-z\right)\partial_{z}^{2}+\left(32z-1\right)\partial_{z}+4 has indicial polynomial z2z^{2} at z=0z=0..

The converse of some of these implications is the object of the following conjecture. Notably, part (3) extends part (2) and gives a converse to Proposition 3 that allows (conjecturally) to detect algebraic solutions of linear differential equations under the global boundedness assumption.

Conjecture 10 (Christol, André).

Let f∈ℚ⁡[[z]]f\in{\mathbb{Q}}[[z]] be a globally bounded and D-finite power series. Then:

  1. (1)

    ff is the diagonal of a rational function;

  2. (2)

    If z=0z=0 is an ordinary point for LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f}, then ff is algebraic;

  3. (3)

    If LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} admits a logarithm-free fundamental system at z=0z=0, then ff is algebraic.

Part (1) of Conjecture 10 is due to Gilles Christol, and was formulated in the late 1980s [23], see also [24, Conj. 4] and [25, Conj. 10]. Part (2) was formulated around 1997 in private discussions between Gilles Christol and Yves André, and appeared in print in [4, Rem. 5.3.2] (there, the connection with the Grothendieck-Katz pp-curvature conjecture is also discussed). See also [77, §3.3] for a similar conjecture (called “Eisenstein’s Algebraicity Criterion” by the author). Part (3) is due to Yves André (private communication).

The global boundedness assumption in Conjecture 10 is crucial for the three parts. For instance, without this assumption, Part (1) does not hold for f⁡(z)=log⁡(1−z)f(z)=\log(1-z), Part (2) does not hold for f⁡(z)=exp⁡(z)f(z)=\exp(z) and Part (3) does not hold for the power series f⁡(z)=F12​[1/6 5/67/6;z]f(z)={}_{2}F_{1}\biggl[\begin{matrix}{1/6\ 5/6}\\ {7/6}\end{matrix}\,;\,z\biggr] considered in [63, Prop. 2.3], which actually is the particular case (a,b)=(1/6,5/6)(a,b)=(1/6,5/6) of the following example.

Example 11.

There exist D-finite transcendental power series whose minimal-order operator is Fuchsian and such that all singular points are algebraic (not logarithmic) singularities. Take aa and bb in ℚ∖ℤ{\mathbb{Q}}\setminus{\mathbb{Z}} such that b−ab-a is not an integer. Then f⁡(z)=F12​[a​ba+1;z]f(z)={}_{2}F_{1}\biggl[\begin{matrix}{a\ b}\\ {a+1}\end{matrix}\,;\,z\biggr] is such that its LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} is reducible, and equals

z(1−z)∂z2+(a+1−(a+b+1)z)∂z−ab=(z(1−z)∂z+1−(b+1)z)(∂z+a/z).z(1-z)\partial_{z}^{2}+(a+1-(a+b+1)z)\partial_{z}-ab=\Big(z(1-z)\partial_{z}+1-(b+1)z\Big)\Big(\partial_{z}+a/z\Big).

Thus, LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} is Fuchsian, it admits the algebraic solution z−az^{-a}, and its local exponents are {0,−a}\{0,-a\} at z=0z=0, {0,1−b}\{0,1-b\} at z=1z=1, {a,b}\{a,b\} at z=∞z=\infty. Since the exponent differences are not integers, the three singularities are algebraic. Moreover, f⁡(z)f(z) is transcendental, since otherwise the operator LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} would have finite cyclic monodromy and this is impossible by [109, Thm. 2.2 (2)]. However, f⁡(z)f(z) is not globally bounded by [23, Prop. 1], so this example does not contradict Part (3) of Conjecture 10.

We design now a more efficient version of Algorithm 1; this is Algorithm 3, based on Propositions 3, 4 and 10.

Theorem 12.

Given a linear differential operator L∈ℚ[z]⟨∂z⟩L\in{\mathbb{Q}}[z]\langle\partial_{z}\rangle and sufficiently many initial conditions specifying a unique solution f∈ℚ⁡[[z]]f\in{\mathbb{Q}}[[z]], every output T of Algorithm 3 is unconditionally correct. If ff is globally bounded, then, assuming Part (3) of Conjecture 10, every output A is also correct.

Proof.

If ff is algebraic, then, by Corollary 4, LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} is Fuchsian and it admits only rational exponents at all its singular points. Moreover, if LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} has a logarithmic singularity at z=0z=0, then ff is transcendental by Proposition 3. This proves the first part of the result. The last part follows from Conjecture 10. ∎

Remark 13.

Example 11 shows that the assumption “f⁡(z)f(z) is globally bounded” is necessary in Algorithm 3, even if we replaced “LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} has a logarithmic singularity at z=0z=0” by “LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} has a logarithmic singularity at one of its singular points”.

Remark 14.

As already mentioned in Section 1.4, it is currently not known how to decide if a given D-finite power series f⁡(z)f(z) is globally bounded. However, this property is known to be satisfied by large classes of power series, such as generating functions of multiple binomial sums or, equivalently, by diagonals of rational functions, see [17, Theorem 3.5]. In this case, the operator LL annihilating ff does not need to be part of the input: it can be computed from a diagonal representation of ff using creative telescoping, see [17] and the references therein (Section 5.2 provides several non-trivial examples). Still in this case, Algorithm 3 can be enhanced in the following way: after computing LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f}, if it detects logarithms in the local basis of solutions of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} at z=0z=0, then it concludes transcendence; if it detects a term logs⁡(z)\log^{s}(z) in that local basis (e.g., if the indicial polynomial of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} at z=0z=0 is zs+1⋅P⁡(z)z^{s+1}\cdot P(z) with P⁡(0)≠0P(0)\neq 0), then it can conclude that the number of variables needed to express f⁡(z)f(z) as the diagonal of a rational function is at least s+2s+2 [49, Corollary 2.7], thus proving a strong form of transcendence of f⁡(z)f(z) if s≥1s\geq 1. For instance, in Example 5, the presence of terms log2⁡(z)\log^{2}(z) in the local basis of LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} at z=0z=0 implies that this number is at least 44 (and in fact exactly 44, e.g., using the diagonal representations in Section A.2), see also [49, Example 3.9].

3. Solving problem (P)

Given an operator L∈ℚ(z)⟨∂z⟩L\in\mathbb{Q}(z)\langle{\partial_{z}}\rangle the aim of this section is to present Algorithm 4 that computes the operator Lalg∈ℚ(z)⟨∂z⟩L^{\mathrm{alg}}\in\mathbb{Q}(z)\langle{\partial_{z}}\rangle whose solution space is spanned by the algebraic solutions of L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0 (see Section 2.1). This is done by extending some of Singer’s results [96, 99]. Algorithm 4 is then used in Algorithm 5 to solve Stanley’s problem (S) in full generality, providing a second proof that Stanley’s problem (S) is decidable.

Both algorithms rely on Singer’s algorithm [96], which suffers from a very large bound, except for very small order, where one can use more refined bounds [67, 54, 102], see Section 1.7. This prevents us from obtaining practical versions of Algorithms 4 and 5. Still, the computation of LalgL^{\mathrm{alg}} is a question of independent interest. We first recall the following definition:

Definition 15.

Let kk be a differential field of characteristic zero and L1,L2∈k⟨∂⟩L_{1},L_{2}\in k\langle\partial\rangle be irreducible operators of order nn. We say L1L_{1} is equivalent to L2L_{2} if there exist a0,a1,…,an−1∈ka_{0},a_{1},\ldots,a_{n-1}\in k, not all zero, such that L1L_{1} divides L2∘(an−1∂n−1+⋯+a0)L_{2}\circ(a_{n-1}\partial^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{0}) on the right.

This is a special case of a more general definition1313 13 Of operators of the same type, whose definition does not require irreducibility. but we will only need this version and the fact that this is an equivalence relation [99, Cor. 2.6]. If KK is a Picard-Vessiot extension of kk containing a full set of solutions of L1​(y)=0L_{1}(y)=0 and of L2​(y)=0L_{2}(y)=0 then the map ϕ:y↦an−1​∂n−1y+⋯+a0​y\phi:y\mapsto a_{n-1}\partial^{n-1}y+\dots+a_{0}y maps the solution space of L1​(y)=0L_{1}(y)=0 to the solution space of L2​(y)=0L_{2}(y)=0. Since L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} are irreducible, this map is a bijection [99, Cor. 2.6]. All solutions of L1​(y)=0L_{1}(y)=0 are algebraic then so are their images by ϕ\phi and therefore the same is true for L2​(y)=0L_{2}(y)=0. The converse is true, since the inverse of the bijection is of the same type.

Algorithm 4 computes LalgL^{\mathrm{alg}} when k=ℚ¯​(z)k={\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(z) and C=ℚ¯C={\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}. Step 4 is performed using any factorization algorithm, e.g., [46], or [57]; step 5 is solved by Singer’s algorithms [96] or [97]; for the computation of the LCLM in step 7, see e.g., [14], or [56]. By Proposition 3, if the input LL is in ℚ(z)⟨∂⟩\mathbb{Q}(z)\langle\partial\rangle, then even if the intermediate computations take place in ℚ¯(z)⟨∂⟩{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(z)\langle\partial\rangle, the output LalgL^{\mathrm{alg}} does belong to ℚ(z)⟨∂⟩\mathbb{Q}(z)\langle\partial\rangle.

We will now justify the equation in the last step and show how one can construct the operator in step 6.

3.1. Proof of the algorithm

This proof uses again concepts from the differential Galois theory of linear differential equations as in Section 2.1. Let kk be a differential field of characteristic 0 with algebraically closed field of constants CC, L∈k⟨∂⟩L\in k\langle\partial\rangle, KK the Picard-Vessiot extension of kk corresponding to L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0 and GG the Galois group of KK over kk.

We recall that the vector space of solutions of L⁡(y)=0L(y)=0 that are algebraic over kk is invariant under GG and so spans the solution space ValgV^{\textrm{alg}} of a linear differential equation Lalg​(y)=0L^{\mathrm{alg}}(y)=0 with Lalg∈k⟨∂⟩L^{\mathrm{alg}}\in k\langle\partial\rangle. Note that LalgL^{\mathrm{alg}} divides LL on the right [99, Lemma 2.1]. The equation Lalg​(y)=0L^{\mathrm{alg}}(y)=0 obviously has a full set of solutions in KK and they generate a Picard-Vessiot extension EE over kk with k⊂E⊂Kk\subset E\subset K. Furthermore the Galois group HH of EE over kk is finite. A finite group acting on a vector space allows one to decompose the vector space as a direct sum of irreducible subspaces. Therefore Valg=⊕iViV^{\textrm{alg}}=\oplus_{i}V_{i}, each ViV_{i} an HH-irreducible space. Furthermore, each ViV_{i} is the solution space of an irreducible Mi∈k⟨∂⟩M_{i}\in k\langle\partial\rangle. Factorizations of linear operators are unique up to equivalence [99, Proposition 2.11]. It follows that MiM_{i} must be equivalent to some LijL_{i_{j}} and so must divide some L^ij\widehat{L}_{i_{j}}. Therefore the solution space of LCLM​{L^i1,…,L^is}​(y)=0\textrm{LCLM}\{\widehat{L}_{i_{1}},\ldots,\widehat{L}_{i_{s}}\}(y)=0 contains the solution space of Lalg​(y)=0L^{\mathrm{alg}}(y)=0. Conversely all solutions of LCLM​{L^i1,…,L^is}​(y)=0\textrm{LCLM}\{\widehat{L}_{i_{1}},\ldots,\widehat{L}_{i_{s}}\}(y)=0 are algebraic so its solution space is contained in the solution space of Lalg​(y)=0L^{\mathrm{alg}}(y)=0. Therefore these monic operators are equal.

3.2. Computing the L^ij\widehat{L}_{i_{j}}

This will follow from

Proposition 16.

Let kk be a differential field of characteristic 0 with algebraically closed field of constants CC and satisfying the following property:

If L∈k⟨∂⟩L\in k\langle\partial\rangle then one can effectively find a CC-basis of the space

{u∈k|L​u=0}.\{u\in k\ |\ Lu=0\}.

Let M,L∈k⟨∂⟩M,L\in k\langle\partial\rangle and assume that MM is irreducible. One can effectively find1414 14 This is a LCLM of a potentially infinite set of operators that are all right divisors of LL. Thus, the earlier definition extends and the LCLM is a right divisor of LL. By convention, if the set is empty, the LCLM is taken to be 1.

M^=LCLM{R∈k⟨∂⟩|R is equivalent to M and divides L on the right}.\widehat{M}=\textrm{\emph{LCLM}}\{R\in k\langle\partial\rangle\ |\ R\text{ is equivalent to }M\text{ and divides }L\text{ on the right}\}.

Note that in the application of this proposition in Algorithm 4, where the field kk is ℚ¯​(z){\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(z), the property is satisfied by Liouville’s algorithm [73], see also [1].

Proof.

Let MM have order nn. The set

W={𝐚=(an−1,…,a0)∈kn|M divides L∘(an−1∂n−1+⋯+a0) on the right}W=\{\mathbf{a}=(a_{n-1},\ldots,a_{0})\in k^{n}\ |\ M\text{ divides }L\circ(a_{n-1}\partial^{n-1}+\dots+a_{0})\text{ on the right}\}

is a vector space over the constants. By computing the product L∘(an−1∂n−1+⋯+a0)L\circ(a_{n-1}\partial^{n-1}+\dots+a_{0}), its right Euclidean division by MM and writing that the remainder is 0, we get an n×nn\times n matrix 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} with entries in k⟨∂⟩k\langle\partial\rangle such that 𝐚∈W\mathbf{a}\in W if and only if 𝒜​𝐚=0{\mathcal{A}}\mathbf{a}=0 (see the discussion following Example 2.8 in [99]). Finding solutions of 𝒜​Y=0{\mathcal{A}}Y=0 in knk^{n} can be reduced to finding solutions of scalar linear differential equations in kk and so one can find a CC-basis {𝐚1,…,𝐚s}\{{\mathbf{a}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbf{a}}_{s}\} of WW [88, Chap. III, §11]. If W={0}W=\{0\}, there is no RR equivalent to MM that divides LL on the right and the result is M^=1\widehat{M}=1.

For 𝐚=(an−1,…,a0)∈W∖{0}{\mathbf{a}}=(a_{n-1},\ldots,a_{0})\in W\setminus\{0\}, we construct an operator L𝐚∈k⟨∂⟩L_{{\mathbf{a}}}\in k\langle\partial\rangle of order at most nn so that the map A𝐚:y↦an−1​∂n−1y+⋯+a0​yA_{\mathbf{a}}:y\mapsto a_{n-1}\partial^{n-1}y+\dots+a_{0}y maps the solution space of MM to the solution space of L𝐚L_{\mathbf{a}}. This is done by differentiating jj times the equality v=an−1​∂n−1y+⋯+a0​yv=a_{n-1}\partial^{n-1}y+\dots+a_{0}y for j=0,…,nj=0,\dots,n and using the equation M​y=0My=0 to express each derivative v(j)v^{(j)} in terms of y,…,∂n−1yy,\ldots,\partial^{n-1}y. The resulting n+1n+1 expressions must be linearly dependent over kk and this yields an equation L𝐚L_{\mathbf{a}}. The operator L𝐚L_{\mathbf{a}} obtained that way has order exactly nn and is irreducible: by its construction, there exists an operator Q1Q_{1} such that L𝐚∘A𝐚=Q1∘ML_{\mathbf{a}}\circ A_{\mathbf{a}}=Q_{1}\circ M with A𝐚A_{\mathbf{a}} relatively prime to MM since MM is irreducible; the conclusion follows from general decomposition theorems [81, Ch. II. Thm. 1], [99, Prop. 2.11]. This shows that L𝐚L_{\mathbf{a}} is equivalent to MM. Moreover, L𝐚L_{\mathbf{a}} divides LL on the right since A𝐚A_{\mathbf{a}} maps the solution space of MM bijectively into the solution space of L𝐚L_{\mathbf{a}}, while it also maps it into the solution space of LL.

Let M~=LCLM​{L𝐚1,…,L𝐚s}{\widetilde{M}}=\textrm{LCLM}\{L_{{\mathbf{a}}_{1}},\ldots,L_{{\mathbf{a}}_{s}}\}. We will show that M~=M^\widetilde{M}=\widehat{M}. Since each L𝐚iL_{{\mathbf{a}}_{i}} is equivalent to MM and divides LL on the right, we have that M~{\widetilde{M}} divides M^{\widehat{M}} on the right.

Now assume that an operator RR is equivalent to MM and divides LL on the right. Let A𝐚=an−1∂n−1+⋯+a0A_{\mathbf{a}}=a_{n-1}\partial^{n-1}+\dots+a_{0} be such that MM divides R∘A𝐚R\circ A_{\mathbf{a}} on the right. Since RR divides LL on the right, we have that MM divides L∘A𝐚L\circ A_{\mathbf{a}} on the right. Therefore 𝐚=(an−1,…,a0)∈W{\mathbf{a}}=(a_{n-1},\ldots,a_{0})\in W and so there exist c1,…,cs∈Cc_{1},\ldots,c_{s}\in C such that 𝐚=∑ci​𝐚i{\mathbf{a}}=\sum c_{i}{\mathbf{a}}_{i}. Moreover, A𝐚A_{\mathbf{a}} maps the solution space of MM bijectively into the solution space of RR. Since A𝐚=∑ci​A𝐚iA_{\mathbf{a}}=\sum{c_{i}A_{{\mathbf{a}}_{i}}}, the latter space is included in the sum of the solution spaces of the L𝐚iL_{{\mathbf{a}}_{i}}, which is the solution space of M~{\widetilde{M}}. Therefore RR divides M~{\widetilde{M}} on the right.

Since M^{\widehat{M}} is the LCLM of all such RR, we have that M^{\widehat{M}} divides M~{\widetilde{M}} on the right. Since both of these operators are monic, we have shown that they are equal. ∎

Remark 17.

Proposition 16 can be used as a building block to construct the Loewy decomposition of an operator into the product of completely reducible operators.

4. Other algorithmic approaches to algebraicity and transcendence

4.1. Using the Grothendieck-Katz pp-curvature conjecture

In the 1970s, Alexander Grothendieck proposed a conjectural “arithmetic” characterization for linear differential operators with coefficients in ℚ⁡(z){\mathbb{Q}}(z): such an operator admits a full basis of algebraic solutions if and only if the same holds for its reductions modulo pp for almost all primes pp. Grothendieck’s conjecture can be seen as a differential generalization of a particular case, due to Kronecker, of Chebotarev’s theorem: the roots of a polynomial in ℚ⁡[z]{\mathbb{Q}}[z] are all rational if and only if the roots of its reductions modulo pp are in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} for almost all primes pp. (See [12, 43], and the references therein.)

Although it remains largely open in the general case, the pp-curvature conjecture has been proven in several important cases. It was first studied in depth and popularized by Nicholas Katz [61], who proved it for the Gauss hypergeometric equations, a result later extended to the generalized hypergeometric equations by Beukers and Heckman [8]. More generally, it was proved in [61] and [4, §III] for Picard-Fuchs differential operators (satisfied by the periods of families of smooth algebraic varieties) and for certain of their direct factors and subquotients (sometimes called “differential equations coming from geometry”). In a different direction, the pp-curvature conjecture was proved by the Chudnovsky brothers [26] (see also [4, §6]) for linear differential operators of first order with algebraic function coefficients in ℚ⁡(z)¯\overline{{\mathbb{Q}}(z)}. (This last arithmetic approach was used to prove the algebraicity of some power series e.g., in [64, 31, 10].)

Consider now problem (F) for any linear differential operator LL for which the Grothendieck-Katz conjecture is known to hold. For any fixed prime pp, the linear differential operator LmodpL\bmod p, with coefficients in 𝔽p​(z)\mathbb{F}_{p}(z), admits a basis of algebraic solutions if and only if it admits a basis of rational solutions [21], and this is verified by a very simple algorithm, based on checking the nullity of the pp-curvature of LL.

In practice, computing pp-curvatures for a few primes pp provides a very efficient heuristic: if LL has several zero pp-curvatures, then it very likely admits a full basis of algebraic solutions. In particular, for problem (S), if the Grothendieck-Katz conjecture is known to hold for LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} and if LfminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f} has several zero pp-curvatures, then f⁡(z)f(z) is very likely algebraic, otherwise it is very likely transcendental. To turn this heuristic into a decision algorithm, one would need an upper bound on the number of primes pp for which the pp-curvature is to be tested. In other words, one needs an effective Grothendieck-Katz theorem, similar to effective versions of Chebotarev’s theorem (e.g., [86] and the references therein). For Picard-Fuchs operators, the existence of such results is alluded to by André [4, §16.3.1]. A first complete effective result was recently obtained, for first-order linear operators with rational function coefficients, by Fürnsinn and Pannier [43]. Much remains to be done in this direction, for more general classes of linear differential operators.

4.2. Guess-and-prove

To prove algebraicity of a given power series f⁡(z)f(z), a very popular method in computer algebra is to first guess a polynomial P⁡(z,u)∈ℚ⁡[z,u]P(z,u)\in{\mathbb{Q}}[z,u] such that P⁡(z,f⁡(z))=O⁡(zσ)P(z,f(z))=O(z^{\sigma}) for some value σ\sigma, and then to certify that P⁡(z,f⁡(z))=0P(z,f(z))=0 by manipulating the roots of PP via the differential operator LPL_{P} whose solution space is generated by these roots. This strategy is explained for instance in the proof of [16, Corollary 2]. The guessing part is based on (structured) linear algebra (over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}) in size σ\sigma and the most efficient algorithms use Hermite-Padé approximants (which reduce the problem to linear algebra over ℚ⁡(z){\mathbb{Q}}(z) in a size much smaller than σ\sigma). The proving part is based on the computation of LPL_{P}, which ultimately also relies on linear algebra [13], and sufficiently many initial conditions. A delicate issue is the choice of σ\sigma; usually one keeps doubling its value and degree bounds on PP until a candidate PP is found. If f⁡(z)f(z) is algebraic, then the procedure will eventually discover it (modulo computational difficulties related to the size of σ\sigma that can be huge).

This approach applies to problem (S) when ff is D-finite. Its strength is that it is able to recognize and prove algebraicity of f⁡(z)f(z) even in situations where f⁡(z)f(z) is not a priori known to be D-finite (e.g., it is given not by an ODE, but by a different kind of functional equation), see e.g., [16]. The weak point of the approach is that it cannot prove that f⁡(z)f(z) is transcendental. This is why it is usually used in conjunction with other heuristics such as computations of pp-curvatures, or numerical computations of local monodromies.

4.3. Factoring

If the input LL is checked to be irreducible, then its solution ff is algebraic if and only if all solutions of LL are algebraic (by Proposition 2.5 in [96]), and this can be tested using Singer’s 1979 algorithm [96]. But if LL is reducible, then it is a priori not clear how to combine factoring algorithms [57, 46] and Singer’s algorithm [96] in order to solve Stanley’s problem (S). One practical way is: factor the input L=A​BL=AB for irreducible AA of order less than the order of LL and check if AA has a basis of algebraic solutions. If yes, then we cannot conclude. (See the examples at the end of Section 5.2.) If no, then AA has no nontrivial algebraic solutions, and there are two possible cases. Either g≔B⁡(f)g\coloneq B(f) is nonzero, in which case it is transcendental (as it is a nontrivial solution of AA), hence ff itself is transcendental (otherwise gg would be algebraic). Or, g=0g=0, and we can repeat the whole procedure on BB. This procedure is guaranteed to succeed in the particular case when LL factors as a product of irreducible operators each of them having no algebraic solutions.

5. Examples

Starting from an implementation of the minimization algorithm [18], the implementation of the transcendence test of Algorithm 2 in Maple is straightforward and fits in 40 lines.1515 15 It is implemented in the function istranscendental in versions later than 4.05 of the package gfun, available at https://perso.ens-lyon.fr/bruno.salvy/software/the-gfun-package/, where a Maple session with these examples can also be found. We list a few experiments performed with this implementation.

5.1. Combinatorial examples

Examples with a combinatorial origin for which our implementation gives an automatic proof of transcendence are:
