  • •

    the 72 transcendental cases from [15, Theorem 2] (in a total of 25 seconds);

  • •

    the lattice Green functions of the face-centered cubic lattice in dimensions d=2,…,11d=2,\dots,11. These (D-finite) functions are defined by

    Gd(z)≔1πd∫0π⋯∫0πdθ1⋯dθd1−z(d2)−1∑1≤i<j≤dcosθicosθj.G_{d}(z)\coloneq\frac{1}{\pi^{d}}\int_{0}^{\pi}\cdots\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{d\theta_{1}\cdots d\theta_{d}}{1-z\binom{d}{2}^{-1}\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq d}\cos\theta_{i}\cos\theta_{j}}.

    When d=2d=2 and d=3d=3, we have hypergeometric expressions [48, Eq. (53)], [60, Eq. (3.6)]

    G2​(z)=F12​[12​121;z2],G3​(z)=F12​[16​131;z2​(z+3)4]2G_{2}(z)={}_{2}F_{1}\biggl[\begin{matrix}{\frac{1}{2}\ \frac{1}{2}}\\ {1}\end{matrix}\,;\,z^{2}\biggr],\quad G_{3}(z)={}_{2}F_{1}\biggl[\begin{matrix}{\frac{1}{6}\ \frac{1}{3}}\\ {1}\end{matrix}\,;\,\frac{z^{2}(z+3)}{4}\biggr]^{2}

    that can be seen to be transcendental by the arguments of Section 1.6. For d≥4d\geq 4, no such closed formulas are known, and it is not clear how to decide transcendence of Gd​(z)G_{d}(z) using asymptotic arguments. Linear differential equations for Gd​(z)G_{d}(z) were first conjectured by Guttmann in dimension 4 [47] and by Broadhurst in dimension 5 [20], after intensive computations. They were then computed by Koutschan for d=3,4,5,6d=3,4,5,6 using creative telescoping [66]. For d=7d=7, an equation was conjectured by Hassani, Maillard and Zenine [112] and then equations were conjectured up to d=11d=11 by Hassani, Koutschan, Maillard and Zenine [50].

    While these differential equations have been obtained after days of computations, it is relatively simple for our code to prove that they are minimal. (Note that their minimality for d≤11d\leq 11, and even their irreducibility for d≤7d\leq 7, were claimed in [50, Section 2.2] and [112, Section 4], but the arguments there are based on heuristics.) Since all these equations are minimal and have a logarithmic singularity at 0, Proposition 3 implies that Gd​(z)G_{d}(z) is transcendental for d≤11d\leq 11 (assuming the conjectured differential equations to be correct for d≥7d\geq 7). Alternatively, one can use factorization of linear differential operators to prove that the differential equations for Gd​(z)G_{d}(z) are irreducible for d≤8d\leq 8, and use Proposition 2.5 in [96] (rather than Proposition 3) to deduce the transcendence of Gd​(z)G_{d}(z). Sizes and timings are reported in Table 1. (The column “transc” indicates the time taken by our code to prove transcendence of Gd​(z)G_{d}(z); the time taken by the factorization program from [27] is given in the column “factor”. Maple’s native command DFactor was much slower.)

In practice, for all these examples, all the time is spent in the first step where a differential equation of certified minimality is computed.

5.2. Diagonals

A classical result by Pólya and Furstenberg states that the diagonal of any bivariate rational function is algebraic [87, 42]. In characteristic 0 and with three or more variables, diagonals need not be algebraic. The examples below illustrate how our methods can prove transcendence and can suggest algebraicity, which may then sometimes be established by a separate argument.

Example 1: an algebraic case

Using Koutschan’s HolonomicFunctions package [65], the diagonal of

1(1−5​x−7​y​z−13​z2)​(1−x−x​y)\frac{1}{(1-5x-7yz-13z^{2})(1-x-xy)}

is found to satisfy a linear differential equation of order 5 with coefficients of degree up to 24. This equation has logarithmic singularities at 0 and 1/1401/140. However, minimization shows that the diagonal actually satisfies an equation of order only 3 with coefficients of degree up to 13. From that equation, Algorithm 3 strongly suggests that the diagonal is algebraic (being a diagonal, it is globally bounded). Actually, the more general situation of the diagonal of

F⁡(x,y,z)=1(1−a​x−b​y​z−c​z2)​(1−x−x​y)F(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{(1-ax-byz-cz^{2})(1-x-xy)}

for arbitrary a,b,ca,b,c can be seen to be algebraic by a direct residue computation: the diagonal is the residue at x=y=0x=y=0 of

G⁡(x,y,z,t)=1x​y​F​(x,y,t/(x​y))=x​y((x−a​x2−b​t)​x​y2−c​t2)​(1−x−x​y)G(x,y,z,t)=\frac{1}{xy}F(x,y,t/(xy))=\frac{xy}{((x-ax^{2}-bt)xy^{2}-ct^{2})(1-x-xy)}

when t→0t\rightarrow 0. The second factor of the denominator has a root in yy that is away from 0 while the first factor has two roots in yy that both tend to 0 when t→0t\rightarrow 0. The sum of their residues is therefore a rational function in x,tx,t. From there it follows that the sum of residues in xx is algebraic. An explicit computation is possible: by a Rothstein-Trager resultant [43, Thm. 2.1], one obtains a polynomial cancelling these two residues in yy, from whose coefficients their sum is deduced to be

x−1a​x4−2​a​x3+b​t​x2+c​t2​x+a​x2−2​b​t​x−x3+b​t+2​x2−x.\frac{x-1}{a\,x^{4}-2a\,x^{3}+bt\,x^{2}+c\,t^{2}x+a\,x^{2}-2btx-x^{3}+bt+2x^{2}-x}.

Only one of the roots of the denominator tends to 0 with tt. Again, a Rothstein-Trager resultant gives a polynomial of degree 4 cancelling the diagonal.

Example 3: a transcendental case with a difficult right factor

Finally, let us consider the diagonal of

1(1−x−y−z2)​(1−x−x​y2).\frac{1}{(1-x-y-z^{2})(1-x-xy^{2})}.

It is annihilated by a linear differential operator L9L_{9} of order 9 and degree 60 that factors2020 20 This operator and its factorization were communicated to us by Jean-Marie Maillard. Another transcendence proof is based on the method in Section 4.3, as above. By contrast, it is much more challenging to prove that all solutions of A5A_{5} are algebraic. The approach using guess-and-prove described in Section 4.2 is applicable in principle: the guessing part is feasible in practice, although computationally very expensive, but the proving step seems to be out of reach, even modulo a prime2121 21 Gilles Villard found a polynomial of degree 120 with coefficients of degree 460 that cancels the reduction modulo pp of a power series with largest valuation among the solutions of A5A_{5}, modulo a large prime p=892901p=892901. Proving that the solutions of such a polynomial are a basis of the reductions modulo pp of the solutions of A5A_{5} is feasible in theory, but is extremely demanding computationally..

5.3. Apéry-like series

For p,q∈ℕ∖{0}p,q\in{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\{0\}, we consider the following generalization of the power series in Example 5:

fp,q​(z)=∑n≥0(∑k=0n(nk)p​(n+kk)q)​zn.f_{p,q}(z)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}^{p}\binom{n+k}{k}^{q}\right)z^{n}.

In Appendix A we use Flajolet’s criterion to prove that fp,q​(z)f_{p,q}(z) is transcendental if and only if (p,q)≠(1,1)(p,q)\neq(1,1). It was conjectured by Sergey Yurkevich in [110, Conjecture 10.5] that the minimal number μp,q\mu_{p,q} of variables needed to represent fp,q​(z)f_{p,q}(z) as the diagonal of a rational power series is equal to p+qp+q. Yurkevich showed that μp,q≤p+q\mu_{p,q}\leq p+q, by using the identity (due to Wadim Zudilin)

(3) fp,q=Diag⁡(1(∏j=1q(1−yj)−x1)⋅∏k=2p(1−xk)−∏k=1pxk⋅∏j=1qyj).f_{p,q}={\operatorname{Diag}}\!\left(\frac{1}{\left(\prod_{j=1}^{q}(1-y_{j})-x_{1}\right)\cdot\prod_{k=2}^{p}(1-x_{k})-\prod_{k=1}^{p}x_{k}\cdot\prod_{j=1}^{q}y_{j}}\right).

For p+q≤10p+q\leq 10, we checked the opposite inequality p+q≤μp,qp+q\leq\mu_{p,q} by using [49, Corollary 2.7] and the enhanced version of our Algorithm 3, mentioned in Remark 14. Indeed, in all these 45 cases, the indicial polynomial Ip,q​(z)I_{p,q}(z) of Lfp,qminL^{\mathrm{min}}_{f_{p,q}} at z=0z=0 equals zp+q−1⋅Rp,q​(z)z^{p+q-1}\cdot R_{p,q}(z) where Rp,q​(0)≠0R_{p,q}(0)\neq 0, hence Yurkevich’s conjecture holds. By looking closely at the indicial polynomials Ip,q​(z)I_{p,q}(z), we made a few additional observations. Appendix A Generalized Apéry series

A.1. A multiple binomial sum

A direct application of Flajolet’s criterion proves the transcendence of the following family of power series, extending the one in Section 5.3.

Proposition 18.

Let (p0,…,pm)∈ℕm+1(p_{0},\dots,p_{m})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{m+1} with p0≥1p_{0}\geq 1. Then the power series

f𝐩​(z)=∑n≥0(∑k=0n(nk)p0​(n+kk)p1​(n+2​kk)p2​⋯​(n+m​kk)pm)​znf_{\mathbf{p}}(z)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}^{p_{0}}\binom{n+k}{k}^{p_{1}}\binom{n+2k}{k}^{p_{2}}\dotsm\binom{n+mk}{k}^{p_{m}}\right)z^{n}

is transcendental if and only if p:=p0+⋯+pm>2p:=p_{0}+\dots+p_{m}>2.

Proof.

The case p>2p>2 is covered by Flajolet’s criterion. Asymptotically, the nnth coefficient S𝐩​(n)S_{\mathbf{p}}(n) of f𝐩​(z)f_{\mathbf{p}}(z) behaves like

(4) S𝐩​(n)∼γ​(π​n)1−p2​βn,n→∞S_{\mathbf{p}}(n)\sim\gamma(\pi n)^{\frac{1-p}{2}}\beta^{n},\quad n\rightarrow\infty

with γ\gamma and β\beta algebraic [78]. If p>2p>2 is odd, the exponent of nn is a negative integer making f𝐩​(z)f_{\mathbf{p}}(z) transcendental; if pp is even, Γ⁡((3−p)/2)\Gamma((3-p)/2) is a rational multiple of π\sqrt{\pi} and thus γ​Γ​((3−p)/2)​π(1−p)/2\gamma\Gamma((3-p)/2)\pi^{(1-p)/2} is an algebraic multiple of π1−p/2\pi^{1-p/2}, which is not algebraic for p>2p>2.

For p=1p=1, the series f(1,0,…,0)f_{(1,0,\dots,0)} is the rational 1/(1−2​z)1/(1-2z).

Finally, for p=2p=2, either p0=2p_{0}=2 and all the other pip_{i} are 0, in which case f𝐩=(1−4z)−1/2f_{\mathbf{p}}=(1-4z)^{-1/2}, or p0=1p_{0}=1, pj=1p_{j}=1 for one j≠0j\neq 0 and all other pip_{i} are 0. In that case, the power series can be seen to be algebraic as the diagonal of a bivariate rational function. Here, the rational function

11−z⁡(1+y)​(y+(1+y)j)=∑n≥0zn​∑k=0n(nk)​yn−k​(1+y)n+j​k,\frac{1}{1-z(1+y)(y+(1+y)^{j})}=\sum_{n\geq 0}z^{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}y^{n-k}(1+y)^{n+jk},

has a Taylor expansion whose coefficient of zn​ynz^{n}y^{n} is the desired

∑k=0n(nk)​(n+j​kk).∎\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}\binom{n+jk}{k}.\qed

A.2. Generic diagonals in more than 2 variables are transcendental

It is well known that the Apéry power series f2,2f_{2,2} can be written as the diagonal of a rational power series in 4 variables, e.g., as the diagonal of 1/((1−x−y)​(1−t−z)−x​y​z​t)1/((1-x-y)(1-t-z)-xyzt) [104, Thm. 1.1] or of 1/(((1−z)​(1−t)−x)​(1−y)−x​y​z​t)1/(((1-z)(1-t)-x)(1-y)-xyzt) (see Section 5.3). From such a diagonal representation, the approach of analytic combinatorics in several variables (ACSV) allows to deduce the asymptotics of the nnth Apéry number AnA_{n} as in Example 5, see e.g., [79, Example 1]. More generally, the generalized Apéry power series fp,qf_{p,q} can be written as the diagonal of a rational power series in m=p+qm=p+q variables with nonnegative coefficients, e.g., via (3). Now, [79, Result 1] states that under certain assumptions that hold generically, the nnth coefficient of the diagonal of a rational power series in mm variables with nonnegative coefficients grows asymptotically like γ​βn​nr\gamma\beta^{n}n^{r} where r=(1−m)/2r=(1-m)/2 and γ/(2​π)r∈ℚ¯\gamma/(2\pi)^{r}\in{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}. (This is coherent with the asymptotics (4) in the proof of Proposition 18.) Combined with Flajolet’s criterion, the formula of [79, Result 1] implies that diagonals of “generic” rational functions with nonnegative coefficients are transcendental if m>2m>2; conversely, the bivariate case is algebraic by the result of Pólya and Furstenberg. Note that the genericity assumption is essential, as shown by the example of the diagonal of 1/(1−x−y−y​z−x​y​z)1/(1-x-y-yz-xyz), equal to f1,1​(z)f_{1,1}(z) which is algebraic by Proposition 18, or by the algebraic examples of Section 5.2.

We are also grateful to Florian Fürnsinn and Sergey Yurkevich, who gave us constructive advice on a first version of the manuscript.
